c.tagline: India's first UNESCO World Heritage city — Gandhi's ashram, carved-wood pols, and Gujarati street food.

taxi.fareNote: Auto-rickshaws are the main street taxi — they have meters, but insist on the meter or agree a price before setting off. App-based Uber and Ola autos and cabs are widely used and usually cheaper and hassle-free.

emergency.note: 112 is India's unified emergency number for police, fire, and ambulance; 108 reaches the state ambulance service directly.

hood_desc: The UNESCO World Heritage walled city, a dense warren of carved wooden pols (traditional housing clusters), the Jama Masjid and Sidi Saiyyed Mosque, Bhadra Fort, and Manek Chowk — a jewelry bazaar by day that turns into a legendary street-food market at night; best for first-timers who want history within walking distance.
A central, buzzing commercial and student district around Gujarat University, packed with cafes, bookshops, offices, and mid-range hotels; a convenient walkable base close to almost everything.

An upscale shopping and dining spine running from CG Road across the Ellisbridge to the Sabarmati Riverfront, lined with malls, boutiques, and restaurants; suits travelers who want retail, riverside walks, and comfort.

The modern western corridor of glass-fronted malls, corporate towers, big cafes and restaurants, and the city's best hotels, with Vastrapur Lake nearby; suits business travelers and those wanting a contemporary, spread-out scene.

A traditional, densely local residential quarter on the east side by Kankaria Lake, with bustling markets, temples, and authentic Gujarati eateries; suits budget travelers wanting an everyday, less touristy feel.

water.note: Tap water is not safe for visitors; use bottled or filtered water, including for brushing teeth.

transit.hours: Metro runs roughly 6:20 AM to 10:05 PM daily; Janmarg BRTS and AMTS city buses run from around 6:00 AM to 11:00 PM.
transit.note: The Ahmedabad Metro (Blue Line east-west and Red Line north-south, with a Yellow Line extension toward Gandhinagar) is the fastest way across the city. The Janmarg BRTS bus-rapid-transit runs in dedicated lanes on major corridors, and the older AMTS city buses fill in the rest. Auto-rickshaws and app cabs cover the gaps.
transit.pay: Metro uses tokens, QR tickets via the app, or the National Common Mobility Card (NCMC); fares run ₹5-25. BRTS and AMTS take cash or smart cards. UPI apps (Google Pay, PhonePe, Paytm) are accepted almost everywhere in the city.

bus: GSRTC intercity buses to other Gujarat cities
train: Ahmedabad Junction (Kalupur), a major Indian Railways hub
Vande Bharat and express trains to Mumbai, Delhi, Vadodara, and Surat

transit.m: Prepaid auto-rickshaw to city center (~20-30 min)
Uber/Ola cab or prepaid taxi to city center (25-35 min)

tip.r: Not customary; rounding up or leaving ~5-10% at nicer restaurants is appreciated. Many sit-down restaurants already add a service charge, so check the bill first.

food.name: Khaman and dhokla
food.desc: Steamed, fermented gram-flour cake, spongy and faintly sweet, finished with a mustard-seed and curry-leaf tempering, green chutney and grated coconut.

places.name: Das Khaman
places.note: City-famous khaman counter; soft, freshly steamed batches sold by weight all day.

places.name: Jani Locho and Khaman House
places.note: Specialist in khaman, locho and dhokla variations; go early while the steamers are running.

places.name: Oswal Restaurant
places.note: Khaman ground fresh from chana dal; open roughly 7am to 9.30pm, so easy to fit in.

food.name: Fafda-jalebi
food.desc: The Amdavadi weekend breakfast: crisp ridged gram-flour fafda with fried chilli and papaya chutney, eaten with hot syrup-soaked jalebi.

places.name: Chandravilas
places.note: Serving the city since 1900 and still the classic address for fafda-jalebi.

places.name: Oswal Restaurant
places.note: An institution built on fafda-jalebi; long queues on Sunday mornings and festival days.

places.name: Gheekanta breakfast stalls
places.note: Old-city breakfast zone; arrive before 9am for fafda, jalebi and sev usal off the stove.

food.name: Gujarati thali
food.desc: An endlessly refilled steel platter: farsan, two or three shaak, dal, kadhi, rotli, rice, pickles, chutneys and a sweet, all sweet-salt-sour at once.

places.name: Agashiye, House of MG
places.note: Rooftop thali in a restored 1920s mansion; the refined version, best booked in advance.

places.name: Vishalla
places.note: Village-style open-air complex with rustic thalis eaten on the floor plus a utensil museum.

places.name: Gordhan Thal
places.note: Big, generous, family-focused thali house that locals use for celebration meals.

food.name: Undhiyu
food.desc: Gujarat's winter showpiece: purple yam, beans, banana and methi muthia slow-cooked upside down with green masala. On menus mainly December to February.

places.name: Vishalla
places.note: Cooks undhiyu in the traditional style through winter; comes with puri and jalebi.

places.name: Gordhan Thal
places.note: Seasonal undhiyu on the thali; ask whether it is on before you sit down.

places.name: Agashiye, House of MG
places.note: Menu changes daily with the season, so undhiyu appears in the winter months.

food.name: Manek Chowk night street food
food.desc: A jewellers' square by day that turns into an open-air food market after 9pm: bhaji pav, ghotala, sandwiches, pav bhaji, kulfi and falooda.

places.name: Manek Chowk night market
places.note: The city's essential after-dark eating; stalls run until well past midnight.

places.name: Asharfi Kulfi
places.note: The long-standing kulfi and falooda stall that most people finish their night with.

places.name: Law Garden khau galli
places.note: Second big evening food street, closer to the new city and slightly calmer.

food.name: Chaas (spiced buttermilk)
food.desc: Thin, salted buttermilk whisked with cumin, ginger and coriander. Gujarat is dry, and chaas is what actually cuts the heat and the sweetness.

places.name: Agashiye, House of MG
places.note: Served in steel tumblers as part of the thali; well spiced and properly cold.

places.name: Gordhan Thal
places.note: Free-flowing chaas with the thali, refilled as often as everything else.

places.name: Law Garden and Manek Chowk carts
places.note: Street vendors sell glasses of chaas and masala chaas for a few rupees.

food.name: Masala chai
food.desc: Ginger, cardamom and clove boiled hard with milk and tea dust, poured into small glasses at kitli stalls that anchor Amdavadi social life.

places.name: Lucky Tea Stall
places.note: Famous cafe built around old graves, with maska bun and chai; a genuine city landmark.

places.name: Chandravilas
places.note: Old-city breakfast house where chai comes with the fafda and jalebi.

places.name: Gheekanta kitli stalls
places.note: Cluster of tea stalls near the old city offices; chai and bun maska from early morning.

food.name: Sugarcane juice and fresh fruit juices
food.desc: Cane crushed to order with ginger and lime, plus seasonal Alphonso mango juice and sweet lime, sold from roadside presses through the hot months.

places.name: Manek Chowk juice carts
places.note: Presses running through the evening market; ask for lime and ginger in the cane juice.

places.name: Law Garden juice stalls
places.note: Line of fruit and cane juice carts that stay busy well into the night.

places.name: CG Road juice bars
places.note: Newer-city juice counters for mango, chikoo and mixed-fruit drinks in season.

landmarks: Sabarmati Ashram
Mahatma Gandhi's riverside residence and headquarters of the independence movement from 1917 to 1930, preserving his living quarters, spinning wheel and letters alongside a museum on the Salt March.
Jama Mosque
A 1424 Friday mosque built by Sultan Ahmad Shah I in yellow sandstone, its 260 pillars and blended Hindu-Jain-Islamic carving marking the high point of the style that defines old Ahmedabad.
Sidi Saiyyed Mosque
A 1573 mosque built by the Abyssinian noble Sidi Saiyyed, famed for ten carved stone jali screens whose intertwined-tree lattice has become the unofficial emblem of Ahmedabad.
Bhadra Fort & Teen Darwaza
Ahmedabad's founding citadel, raised by Sultan Ahmad Shah I in 1411 above the Sabarmati, its royal palaces and gates now a restored cultural centre beside the triple-arched Teen Darwaza gateway.
Kankaria Lake
A polygonal artificial lake built in 1451 by Sultan Qutb-ud-Din Ahmad Shah, ringed by a 2.5-kilometre promenade, a zoo and an amusement park, and busiest in the evenings.
Sabarmati Riverfront
An eleven-kilometre landscaped promenade built along both banks since 2012, with 31 ghats, gardens and cycle tracks replacing what had been the river's exposed, flood-prone banks.
Adalaj Stepwell
A five-storey stepwell built in 1499 by Queen Rudabai in Indo-Islamic style, its octagonal shaft and carved pillars descending underground to keep the water cool, 19 kilometres north of the centre.
Hutheesing Jain Temple
A marble Jain temple completed in 1848 by a wealthy merchant family and dedicated to the fifteenth tirthankara, its carved facade and detached triple-arched torana blending temple and haveli styles.
Calico Museum of Textiles

A museum founded in 1949 by the Sarabhai family in a former haveli, holding one of the world's foremost collections of historic Indian textiles including Mughal court tents; entry is by guided tour only.
Sarkhej Roza

A 15th-century mosque, tomb and stepped-tank complex built for the Sufi saint Ganj Bakhsh, seven kilometres southwest of the old city, its geometric pavilions often cited as an influence on Le Corbusier.

train.note: No international trains. Ahmedabad Junction (Kalupur) is the main station, with Vande Bharat and Shatabdi services to Mumbai in about five to six hours and Rajdhani trains to Delhi overnight. The Mumbai-Ahmedabad bullet train is under construction and not expected before the late 2020s. Book on IRCTC 60 days ahead.

bus.note: No international coaches. GSRTC (https://www.gsrtc.in/) runs from Geetamandir bus terminal across Gujarat to Vadodara, Rajkot, Bhuj and Udaipur, and private AC sleeper operators to Mumbai and Jaipur are bookable through redBus (https://www.redbus.in/). The overnight sleeper to Mumbai takes 10-12 hours.

ferry.note: Ahmedabad is inland on the Sabarmati, which is dammed through the city as a riverfront promenade rather than a navigable waterway, so there are no ferries. The Ghogha-Hazira RoPax ferry across the Gulf of Khambhat runs from the coast about 200 km to the south.
